I'm Yamini, and when Vaibhav told me he'd got the internship at the software firm, I said "Wow, that's amazing!" and hugged him in the corridor, my face smiling on its own. Inside I felt small. I had applied to the same firm and heard nothing.

That night I texted him "So proud of you 🎉" and meant it, mostly. Then I lay awake admitting to myself, only to myself, that I was jealous. What surprised me was that the envy pointed at something: I didn't actually want that firm, I wanted work where I build things, and I'd been applying by default.

Two days later I told Vaibhav I'd been a little jealous and was still glad for him. He laughed and said he'd been jealous of my grades for a year.

qa.q: What did Yamini text Vaibhav that night?
qa.a: "So proud of you", with a party emoji.

qa.q: What was Yamini feeling behind the smile in the corridor, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Small and jealous. The smile felt automatic, and Yamini later lay awake admitting the envy privately.

qa.q: How did Yamini use the envy well?
qa.a: Yamini admitted it privately, congratulated Vaibhav honestly and used the feeling to see what work Yamini actually wanted.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav react to the confession, and what does that show?
qa.a: He laughed and said he had been jealous of Yamini's grades for a year, so the honesty made the friendship feel more equal. 🙂

grounding: A friend gets the offer while Yamini has heard nothing; Yamini smiles while feeling small, admits the envy privately, congratulates honestly and clarifies what Yamini wants.

Rain hammered the bus shelter, and the last bus home was ten minutes away. Manjula had hoped to tell Shreya her news properly; now the words came out fast. "I got the research fellowship."

Shreya kept her eyes on the road. "Oh. The great scholar. Should I curtsy?" The joke had a sharp edge.

Manjula felt her cheeks warm. She nearly said, "It's tiny, honestly, anyone could have got it," as she had with others. She stopped. "I'm really happy about it," she said. "And I know these last months have been rough for you. I'm not going anywhere."

Shreya said nothing. She pulled her dupatta over her head and climbed onto the bus, sitting one row ahead. But at the station, she held the umbrella over both of them.

qa.q: How long until the last bus home?
qa.a: Ten minutes.

qa.q: What did Manjula nearly say, and why did she stop?
qa.a: She nearly said the fellowship was tiny, as if shrinking her news would keep Shreya comfortable. She stopped and chose honesty about being happy.

qa.q: What could Manjula do next to keep the friendship warm?
qa.a: Give Shreya room, stay kind, and ask about Shreya's own plans when Shreya seems ready, without hiding her own progress.

qa.q: How might Shreya have felt at the bus shelter?
qa.a: Probably left behind or envious, with the sharp joke covering a sting. Holding the umbrella over both of them suggests she still cares.

grounding: Manjula's success makes her friend Shreya sarcastic and distant; Manjula stays warm without downplaying herself and gives room.

Anand read the result list twice with his finger under the roll numbers. Disha's was there. His was not.

He whooped anyway and lifted Disha off the ground in front of the tea stall while the chai-wallah clapped. He bought a full box of laddoos from the sweet shop and handed them round to the whole coaching class.

On the way home, wheeling his cycle beside Disha, his grin loosened. "I'm properly happy for you," he said. "But my chest is heavy too. Both are true."

Disha took that in. "I know. I'd feel the same. Come to the library tomorrow, we'll go through your paper together."

Anand pedalled slower, still smiling, still sore, and decided that tonight he would sit with his own result instead of pretending it wasn't there.

qa.q: What did Anand buy from the sweet shop?
qa.a: A full box of laddoos.

qa.q: What two feelings did Anand say he had on the way home?
qa.a: He was properly happy for Disha, and his chest was heavy about his own result.

qa.q: What did Anand do wisely?
qa.a: He celebrated fully, then said out loud that he also felt heavy instead of pretending the feeling was absent.

qa.q: How might Disha have felt hearing Anand's words?
qa.a: Probably trusted and relieved. Disha said "I know. I'd feel the same" and offered to go through Anand's paper together. 🙂

grounding: Anand is honestly happy for his friend Disha's success while admitting his own hard feelings.

In the library at Manchester, Chen kept a small table in his notebook: Oskar's class rank, Oskar's internship offers, Oskar's package from the consulting firm, and a column for himself. The gap always ran the wrong way.

On Thursday Oskar left a folder of lecture notes on the desk and went for coffee. Chen looked at the folder for a long time. The old thought came: he could simply not mention the exam summary he'd found in the shared drive.

Instead he tore out the table page and wrote one line at the top of a fresh one: "Better than last month on thermodynamics."

When Oskar came back, Chen said, "The summary is in the blue tab. Use it." Oskar blinked. "Swap mock papers tonight?" They did, and later argued cheerfully about a question neither could solve.

qa.q: What did Chen keep in his notebook?
qa.a: A small table comparing Oskar's rank, offers and package with a column for himself.

qa.q: What was going on in Chen's mind as he looked at the folder?
qa.a: Rivalry and envy. The old thought came that he could simply not mention the exam summary he had found.

qa.q: What does Chen's new one-line note do for him?
qa.a: It shifts the comparison to his own progress since last month, a fairer measure than Oskar's ranks and packages.

qa.q: How might Oskar have felt when Chen shared the summary?
qa.a: Surprised and glad. Asking to swap mock papers treats Chen as a fellow traveller rather than a rival.

grounding: Chen measures himself against Oskar in ranks and packages, then compares with his own yesterday and shares instead of hiding notes.

I'm Rashmi, and I was at the next table in the canteen when Jyoti said to Ankita, "You've got it easy. An offer letter, and you still complain?" Ankita put down her fork. I expected an argument.

Instead Ankita said, "That sounds like a heavy month for you. Tell me." Jyoti talked for a long time about three rejections and an interview where the words simply froze. Ankita listened, then said, "The offer doesn't mean it's been simple. I'm sleeping badly and I'm scared of the job itself." No speech about working harder.

Later Ankita asked, "Want to do a mock interview on Saturday?" Jyoti shrugged, then said okay. I can't tell what Jyoti felt in the moment, but the shoulders came down.

qa.q: What did Ankita offer to do on Saturday?
qa.a: A mock interview with Jyoti.

qa.q: What might Jyoti have been feeling when saying "You've got it easy", and what is uncertain?
qa.a: Discouraged and possibly envious after three rejections and a frozen interview. Rashmi can only see behaviour, so it cannot be known for sure.

qa.q: What did Ankita do that helped?
qa.a: Ankita listened first, shared an honest difficulty of their own, and offered specific help without pity or a lecture.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Ankita to be told, "You've got it easy"?
qa.a: Probably stinging and misunderstood, yet Ankita chose to hear Jyoti out and admitted to sleeping badly and feeling scared.

grounding: A struggling friend feels Ankita has it easier; Ankita listens, shares honestly about own difficulty and offers help without pity, seen by an observer.

passage:
By the third evening the steel plates in the paying-guest room were still unwashed, and Arohi's speaker was playing Bhojpuri songs at eleven while Hansa had a test. Hansa's green dupatta had gone missing too. Hansa felt her fury rising as she filled the bucket at the hand pump, and she wanted to stick a sharp note on the wall.

Instead she counted to ten, waited until morning, and sat on the cot with two cups of tea. "Arohi, I'm getting angry over small things and I don't want that. Can we make a rota for dishes, switch the speaker off by ten on test days, and ask before taking each other's things?"

Arohi rubbed her eyes. "I didn't realise it was piling up. Yes."

They wrote the rota on the back of a calendar and pinned it above the water pot.

qa.q: Where did Hansa and Arohi pin the rota?
qa.a: Above the water pot.

qa.q: What was Hansa feeling as she filled the bucket, and what did she decide not to do?
qa.a: Furious. She wanted to stick a sharp note on the wall but chose to wait and talk in the morning.

qa.q: Why did Hansa's approach work better than a passive-aggressive note?
qa.a: She raised it calmly, over tea, with specific requests and shared rules, so Arohi could agree without feeling attacked.

qa.q: How did Arohi seem to see the situation?
qa.a: Arohi hadn't realised the problems were piling up, which suggests the calm talk let Arohi say yes without getting defensive.

grounding: Dishes, noise and borrowed things build into anger for Hansa, who raises it calmly with specific requests and shared rules.

passage:
"You're impossible to live with, Dilnaz," Maria said, shutting her almirah harder than needed. The bang rang down the hostel corridor of the small-town women's college, over the hum of the generator outside.

Dilnaz's first instinct was to run to the girls next door and complain. Her face went hot. Instead she sat on her bed with her hands under her knees. "Tell me what I do," she said.

Maria listed it: lights on until two, wet towels on Maria's bed, friends staying past visiting hours. Some of it stung and some felt unfair, but the towels part was true.

"I'm sorry about the towels and the lights. I'll fix those. The visiting hours, can we talk about that one? My friends only come on Sundays."

Maria let out a breath. "Okay. Sundays is fine."

qa.q: Which complaint did Dilnaz recognise as true?
qa.a: The wet towels on Maria's bed.

qa.q: What was Dilnaz feeling and wanting when Maria snapped at her, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Hot-faced and defensive, wanting to run to the girls next door and complain, but Dilnaz chose to sit still and ask what the problem was.

qa.q: What did Dilnaz do well in answering the complaint?
qa.a: Dilnaz listened, owned what was true, apologised for it and negotiated the visiting hours instead of getting defensive.

qa.q: How might Maria have felt when Dilnaz asked "Tell me what I do"?
qa.a: Probably surprised and relieved to be heard. Letting out a breath and agreeing to Sundays suggests the tension eased.

grounding: Dilnaz is told she is the difficult roommate, listens for what is true, apologises where needed and negotiates.

passage:
Saturday, late. Third time this month something has gone missing from my shelf: first a charger, then some cash from my envelope, now my good headphones. My stomach has been in a knot all evening.

Madhav is the obvious one. He's the only other person with a key, and he's been strangely cheerful. I typed a message to the whole floor and deleted it. I have no proof. Anyone could walk in when the door isn't latched, and I forgot the latch twice last week.

So tomorrow I'll write down what went missing and when, keep the latch on, and ask Madhav plainly whether he's seen or borrowed anything. If it keeps happening I'll take my list to the warden. I won't accuse him without something solid.

Darshan

qa.q: What has gone missing from Darshan's shelf this month?
qa.a: A charger, some cash from the envelope and the good headphones.

qa.q: Why did Darshan delete the message meant for the whole floor?
qa.a: Darshan has no proof and does not want to accuse Madhav unfairly, since anyone could walk in when the door isn't latched.

qa.q: What plan does Darshan make for tomorrow?
qa.a: Write down what went missing and when, keep the latch on, ask Madhav plainly, and go to the warden with the list if it continues.

qa.q: How might Madhav feel if Darshan had accused him in front of the floor without evidence?
qa.a: If he is innocent, probably hurt and defensive, and the friendship would take damage that is hard to undo.

grounding: Darshan's things and money go missing; Darshan gathers facts, plans to talk to the roommate and involve the warden, and refuses to accuse without evidence.

passage:
Uday had been seeing Rhea for two months, and he wanted her to come to the Pune flat for dinner on Saturday and stay late. He had almost just done it, because Harsha never said anything about anything. But that morning he caught himself: silence wasn't the same as being fine.

Over tea he said, "Rhea's coming Saturday evening. Are you okay with that? And should we agree on a rule for guests, like telling each other a day ahead?"

Harsha lowered the newspaper. "Honestly, I have a design deadline Saturday and I'd like the flat quiet till nine. After that's fine."

"Done. And when your cousins visit, I get the same warning."

They wrote "Guests: message a day before. Quiet hours 10 pm" on the fridge whiteboard. Uday felt lighter, and a bit silly for nearly skipping it.

qa.q: What did Uday and Harsha write on the fridge whiteboard?
qa.a: "Guests: message a day before. Quiet hours 10 pm."

qa.q: Why did Uday decide to ask Harsha instead of just inviting Rhea?
qa.a: He realised that Harsha's silence didn't mean being fine, and felt a bit silly for nearly skipping the conversation.

qa.q: What does the whiteboard rule do for the two flatmates?
qa.a: It makes expectations clear for both, so neither has to assume the other doesn't mind.

qa.q: What did Harsha need that Uday might not have known?
qa.a: A quiet flat until nine on Saturday because of a design deadline.

grounding: Uday wants to bring his partner over and agrees guest and quiet-hour rules with his roommate beforehand instead of assuming.

Dhruv: Yes!! And I need to tell you what happened in the lab today 😅

qa.a: Disappointed. Yogesh answers "Oh. ...okay" and admits hoping they would do everything together.

qa.q: What small step shows Yogesh keeping some independence from Dhruv?
